subject: English
title: Word classes and sentences
body:
WORD CLASSES
• Noun: a person, place or thing (Maya, school, courage)
• Verb: an action or state (run, is, decided)
• Adjective: describes a noun (tired dog, steep hill)
• Adverb: describes a verb, often ends in -ly (slowly, quietly, soon)
• Pronoun: replaces a noun (she, it, they)
• Preposition: shows where or when (under, after, through)
• Conjunction: joins clauses (and, but, because, although)

SENTENCE TYPES
• Simple: one main clause. "The cat slept."
• Compound: two main clauses joined by and/but/or. "The cat slept and the dog barked."
• Complex: a main clause + a subordinate clause. "Although it was late, the cat refused to sleep."

ACTIVE AND PASSIVE
Active: The chef cooked the meal.
Passive: The meal was cooked by the chef.
Use the passive to put the focus on what happened, not who did it.

WRITE BETTER SENTENCES
Vary how you start: with an adverb (Slowly, …), a subordinate clause (When the bell rang, …) or a verb ending in -ing (Clutching her bag, …).

questions.question: Which word is a pronoun? "Maya gave it to them yesterday."
questions.explanation: 'Them' replaces a noun, so it is a pronoun (as is 'it').

questions.question: Which word is a preposition? "The cat hid under the table."
questions.explanation: 'Under' shows where the cat is in relation to the table.

questions.question: Which is a compound sentence?
options: Because the dog barked, the baby woke up.
The dog barked and the baby woke up.
questions.answer: The dog barked and the baby woke up.
questions.explanation: Two main clauses joined by 'and' make a compound sentence.

questions.question: What word class is "happiness"?
questions.explanation: Happiness is a feeling you cannot touch: an abstract noun.

subject: English
title: Punctuation and spelling
body:
APOSTROPHES
• Missing letters: do not → don't, it is → it's
• Belonging: the girl's bag (one girl), the girls' bags (more than one)
• its = belonging to it (no apostrophe). it's = it is / it has.

SPEECH MARKS
"Where are you going?" asked Tom.
• Punctuation goes inside the speech marks
• New speaker, new line

COMMAS
• In lists: eggs, flour, sugar and butter
• After a fronted adverbial: After lunch, we went outside.
• Around extra information: My brother, who is twelve, loves football.

SEMICOLONS AND COLONS
• Semicolon joins two linked main clauses: It was getting dark; we headed home.
• Colon introduces a list or explanation: You need three things: a pen, a ruler and a calculator.

TRICKY SPELLINGS
definitely (de-FINITE-ly), separate (there's A RAT in sepARATe), necessary (one Collar, two Sleeves), their / there / they're, your / you're

questions.question: In "When the rain stopped, we went outside", which part is the subordinate clause?
questions.explanation: 'When the rain stopped' cannot stand alone; it depends on the main clause.

questions.question: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: My sister who is ten, likes swimming.
My sister, who is ten, likes swimming.
My, sister who is ten likes swimming.
My sister who, is ten likes swimming.
questions.answer: My sister, who is ten, likes swimming.
questions.explanation: Extra information in the middle of a sentence needs a comma on both sides.

questions.question: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: 'Children' is already plural, so add 's for possession: children's.

questions.question: What does r"they're" mean?
questions.explanation: They're is short for 'they are'.

subject: English
title: Reading: inference and language
body:
INFERENCE = READING BETWEEN THE LINES
Writers often SHOW feelings instead of telling you.
"She clutched her bag so tightly her knuckles turned white." → she is nervous.
Ask: what does this detail suggest? How do I know?

ANSWERING READING QUESTIONS (P.E.E.)
• Point: Maya feels nervous at first.
• Evidence: "clutching the straps … so tightly that her knuckles turned white"
• Explain: the tight grip shows she is tense and anxious about starting school.

LANGUAGE TECHNIQUES
• Simile: compares using like/as. "as fast as a cheetah"
• Metaphor: says something IS something else. "a river of blazers"
• Personification: gives human qualities to objects. "the wind howled"
• Alliteration: same starting sound. "silent, silver stars"
• Onomatopoeia: words that sound like the noise. crash, shriek, buzz

WHY WORD CHOICE MATTERS
Ask why the writer chose THIS word. "Shrieked" (not "rang") makes the bell sound loud and alarming.

PURPOSE: PIE
Persuade (offers, exclamations, "you"), Inform (facts, headings), Entertain (stories, description). Instructions use commands: "Mix the flour."

questions.question: "The classroom was a zoo." What does this metaphor suggest?
options: The class was noisy and wild
questions.answer: The class was noisy and wild
questions.explanation: Comparing the class to a zoo suggests chaos and noise.

questions.question: "The bees buzzed busily." Which TWO techniques are used?
questions.explanation: Repeated 'b' sounds (alliteration) and 'buzzed' sounds like the noise (onomatopoeia).

questions.question: r"I've told you a million times!" This is an example of ...
questions.explanation: It is a deliberate exaggeration for effect: hyperbole.

questions.question: A writer says a character 'slammed the door and stomped upstairs'. What does this SHOW rather than tell?
questions.explanation: The actions reveal anger without the writer stating it.

subject: Maths
title: Algebra basics
body:
WORDS TO KNOW
• Term: $3a$, $5$, $-2b$
• Expression: terms added or subtracted, e.g. $3a + 5b - 2$ (no equals sign)
• Equation: has an equals sign and can be solved, e.g. $2x + 5 = 17$

SIMPLIFYING (collect like terms)
Only combine terms with the same letter.
$3a + 5b - a + 2b = 2a + 7b$

SUBSTITUTION
Swap the letter for the number, then follow BIDMAS.
If $x = 4$: $3x^2 = 3 \times 16 = 48$  (square first, then multiply)

SOLVING ONE- AND TWO-STEP EQUATIONS
Do the same thing to both sides, undoing in reverse order.
$2x + 5 = 17$
subtract 5: $2x = 12$
divide by 2: $x = 6$
Check: $2 \times 6 + 5 = 17$ ✓

SEQUENCES
3, 7, 11, 15, … goes up by 4 each time.
$n$th term: $4n - 1$  (the times-table of the difference, then adjust)

questions.question: Work out $5 + 3 \times (6 - 2)^2$.
questions.explanation: Brackets: $6 - 2 = 4$. Index: $4^2 = 16$. Multiply: $3 \times 16 = 48$. Add: $5 + 48 = 53$.

questions.question: Which expression means 'multiply n by 4, then subtract 3'?
questions.explanation: Multiplying n by 4 gives $4n$; then subtract 3: $4n - 3$.

questions.question: Simplify $3a \times 4b$.
questions.explanation: Multiply the numbers ($3 \times 4 = 12$) and write the letters together: $12ab$.

questions.question: I think of a number, double it and add 7. The answer is 31. What was my number?

subject: Maths
title: Angles, area and perimeter
body:
ANGLE FACTS
• Angles on a straight line add up to 180°
• Angles around a point add up to 360°
• Angles in a triangle add up to 180°
• Vertically opposite angles are equal

Example: a triangle has angles 48° and 75°. Third angle = $180 - 48 - 75 = 57$°

TYPES OF ANGLE
acute: less than 90°   right: 90°   obtuse: between 90° and 180°   reflex: more than 180°

PERIMETER
The distance all the way around. Add every side.

AREA
• Rectangle: length × width
• Triangle: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times$ base × perpendicular height
• Parallelogram: base × perpendicular height

Example: triangle, base 10 cm, height 6 cm → $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 6 = 30$ cm²

UNITS
Perimeter is in cm; area is in cm² (squared units).

questions.question: An isosceles triangle has one angle of 40° between its two equal sides. What is each of the other two angles?
questions.explanation: $180 - 40 = 140$, shared equally: 70° each.

questions.question: Two straight lines cross. One of the angles is 58°. What is the angle vertically opposite it?
questions.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal: 58°.

questions.question: Angles around a point are 95°, 120° and $x$. Find $x$.
questions.explanation: Angles around a point add to 360°: $360 - 95 - 120 = 145$°.

questions.question: Which of these is a reflex angle?
questions.explanation: Reflex angles are between 180° and 360°.

subject: Maths
title: Fractions, decimals and percentages
body:
KEY IDEA
Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways of writing the same amount.
$\dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5 = 50\%$     $\dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25 = 25\%$     $\dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75 = 75\%$     $\dfrac{1}{10} = 0.1 = 10\%$     $\dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2 = 20\%$

CONVERTING
• Fraction → decimal: divide the top by the bottom. $\dfrac{3}{8} = 3 \div 8 = 0.375$
• Decimal → percentage: multiply by 100. $0.375 = 37.5\%$
• Percentage → fraction: put it over 100 and simplify. $35\% = \dfrac{35}{100} = \dfrac{7}{20}$

ADDING FRACTIONS
Make the denominators the same first.
$\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{8}{12} + \dfrac{3}{12} = \dfrac{11}{12}$

FRACTION OF AN AMOUNT
Divide by the bottom, multiply by the top.
$\dfrac{3}{5}$ of 40: $40 \div 5 = 8$, then $8 \times 3 = 24$

PERCENTAGE OF AN AMOUNT (no calculator)
Build it from 10% and 5%.
15% of 60: 10% = 6, 5% = 3, so 15% = 9

COMMON MISTAKE
Adding the tops and the bottoms: $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}$ is NOT $\dfrac{2}{5}$. It is $\dfrac{3}{6} + \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{5}{6}$.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{5}{8}$ of 72.
questions.explanation: $72 \div 8 = 9$, then $9 \times 5 = 45$.

questions.question: Simplify $\dfrac{18}{24}$ fully.
questions.explanation: The highest common factor of 18 and 24 is 6: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

questions.question: Write $\dfrac{7}{20}$ as a percentage.
Work out $\dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{1}{6}$.
questions.explanation: Common denominator 12: $\dfrac{9}{12} - \dfrac{2}{12} = \dfrac{7}{12}$.

subject: Maths
title: Negative numbers
body:
ON THE NUMBER LINE
Numbers to the left are smaller: $-7 < -2 < 0 < 3$.
Think of temperatures: $-7$°C is colder than $-2$°C.

ADDING AND SUBTRACTING
• Adding a positive: move right. $-4 + 9 = 5$
• Subtracting a positive: move left. $3 - 8 = -5$
• Two signs next to each other:
  $+\,-$ or $-\,+$ → minus.  $6 + (-2) = 6 - 2 = 4$
  $-\,-$ → plus.  $5 - (-3) = 5 + 3 = 8$

MULTIPLYING AND DIVIDING
Same signs → positive. Different signs → negative.
$-3 \times -6 = 18$     $-20 \div 4 = -5$     $7 \times -2 = -14$

CHECK YOURSELF
$-2 - 5 = ?$   (answer: $-7$)
$-12 \div -3 = ?$   (answer: 4)

questions.question: Work out $-7 + 3$.
questions.explanation: Start at $-7$ and move 3 to the right: $-4$.

questions.question: Work out $2 - (-5)$.
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: $2 + 5 = 7$.

questions.question: Work out $-24 \div -6$.
questions.explanation: Same signs give a positive answer: $24 \div 6 = 4$.

questions.question: At 6 am the temperature was $-3$°C. By 2 pm it was 8°C. By how much did it rise?
questions.explanation: From $-3$ up to 0 is 3, then up to 8 is 8 more: $3 + 8 = 11$°C.

subject: Science
title: Cells
body:
ALL LIVING THINGS ARE MADE OF CELLS

ANIMAL AND PLANT CELLS BOTH HAVE
• Nucleus: contains DNA, controls the cell
• Cell membrane: controls what goes in and out
• Cytoplasm: jelly where chemical reactions happen
• Mitochondria: where respiration releases energy

ONLY PLANT CELLS HAVE
• Cell wall: made of cellulose, keeps the cell rigid
• Chloroplasts: where photosynthesis happens (contain green chlorophyll)
• Permanent vacuole: filled with cell sap, keeps the cell firm

LEVELS OF ORGANISATION
cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
e.g. muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system → you

SPECIALISED CELLS
• Red blood cell: no nucleus, more room to carry oxygen
• Root hair cell: long and thin to absorb water
• Sperm cell: tail to swim

USING A MICROSCOPE
Start on the lowest power, focus with the coarse knob, then the fine knob.

questions.question: What is the cell wall of a plant cell made of?
questions.explanation: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, which keeps the cell rigid.

questions.question: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?
options: To have more room to carry oxygen
questions.answer: To have more room to carry oxygen
questions.explanation: Without a nucleus there is more space for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.

questions.question: What does the nucleus contain?
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds DNA, the instructions that control the cell.

questions.question: Which cell part is the site of respiration?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria release energy from glucose by respiration.

subject: Science
title: Forces and energy
body:
FORCES
A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).
Contact forces: friction, air resistance, tension, normal (support) force
Non-contact forces: gravity (weight), magnetism, static electricity

RESULTANT FORCE
• Same direction: add.  Opposite directions: subtract.
10 N right and 4 N left → resultant 6 N to the right.
• Balanced forces (resultant 0): the object stays still or keeps moving at the same speed.

MASS AND WEIGHT
Mass is the amount of matter (kg) and does not change.
Weight is the force of gravity (N): weight = mass × gravitational field strength
On Earth $g \approx 10$ N/kg, so a 50 kg pupil weighs 500 N. On the Moon they weigh about one sixth as much.

ENERGY STORES
kinetic (moving), gravitational (high up), elastic (stretched), chemical (food, fuel, batteries), thermal (hot), nuclear
Energy is never used up; it is transferred between stores.

RENEWABLE vs NON-RENEWABLE
Renewable: wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric, geothermal
Non-renewable: coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear

questions.question: Two people push a box the same way with 30 N and 45 N. What is the resultant force?
questions.explanation: Forces in the same direction add: $30 + 45 = 75$ N.

questions.question: A car's engine pushes it forward with 900 N. Friction and air resistance total 900 N. What happens?
options: It keeps moving at a steady speed
questions.answer: It keeps moving at a steady speed
questions.explanation: The forces are balanced (resultant 0 N), so the speed does not change.

questions.question: Which of these is a non-contact force?
questions.explanation: Gravity acts without touching. Friction, air resistance and tension are contact forces.

questions.question: A bag has a mass of 4 kg. Taking $g = 10$ N/kg, what is its weight?
questions.explanation: Weight = mass × $g$ = $4 \times 10 = 40$ N.

subject: Science
title: Particles and states of matter
body:
THE PARTICLE MODEL
Everything is made of tiny particles. How they are arranged decides the state.

SOLID: particles touching, in a regular pattern, vibrate on the spot. Fixed shape, cannot be squashed.
LIQUID: particles touching but arranged randomly, can slide past each other. Flows, takes the shape of its container, cannot be squashed.
GAS: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions. Fills its container, can be squashed.

CHANGES OF STATE
solid → liquid: melting
liquid → gas: boiling / evaporating
gas → liquid: condensing
liquid → solid: freezing
solid → gas: subliming

DIFFUSION
Particles spread out from where there are lots to where there are few. It is faster in gases and when hotter.

MIXTURES
• Filtration: separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (sand and water)
• Evaporation: gets a dissolved solid back (salt from salty water)
• Chromatography: separates coloured dyes in ink

questions.question: What is the change from gas to liquid called?
questions.explanation: Gas to liquid is condensing, e.g. water droplets forming on a cold window.

questions.question: Ice melts at 0°C. What happens to the particles as the ice melts?
options: They gain energy and break out of their fixed positions
questions.answer: They gain energy and break out of their fixed positions
questions.explanation: Heat gives the particles energy; they break free of the fixed pattern and can move past each other.

questions.question: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
options: Evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature below boiling point
Boiling happens only at the surface
questions.answer: Evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature below boiling point
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at its boiling point.

questions.question: Which statement about liquids is true?
options: They take the shape of their container
questions.answer: They take the shape of their container
questions.explanation: Liquid particles touch but can slide past each other, so liquids flow and take their container's shape.

subject: English
title: Analysing language and structure
body:
LANGUAGE: ZOOM IN ON WORDS
Ask: what does this word make me picture or feel? Why THIS word?
"the river had swallowed the lower field" → personification: the river seems hungry and powerful.

TECHNIQUES TO SPOT
• Pathetic fallacy: weather matches mood (storm = chaos, sunshine = hope)
• Oxymoron: opposites together (deafening silence)
• Semantic field: a group of related words (blood, wound, battle → a field of war)
• Sibilance: repeated 's' sounds (slithering, silent snake)

STRUCTURE: ZOOM OUT
• How does it open and end? Short sentences = impact.
• Does the focus shift (wide view → one detail)?
• Is there a turning point?

WRITING ABOUT IT (P.E.E.)
Point: The writer shows the storm's power.
Evidence: the fence lay "like matchsticks".
Explain: matchsticks are tiny and fragile, so the reader sees how easily the storm destroyed it.

questions.question: What is pathetic fallacy?
options: Weather or setting reflecting a character's mood
questions.answer: Weather or setting reflecting a character's mood
questions.explanation: e.g. rain and grey skies when a character is sad.

questions.question: Which is an oxymoron?
questions.explanation: An oxymoron puts opposite ideas together: deafening + silence.

questions.question: What does "reluctant" mean?
questions.explanation: Reluctant means not wanting to do something.

questions.question: Which word is an antonym (opposite) of "generous"?
questions.explanation: Selfish is the opposite of generous.

subject: English
title: Grammar and persuasive writing
body:
ACTIVE AND PASSIVE
Active: The ball broke the window.
Passive: The window was broken by the ball.

PUNCTUATION FOR EFFECT
• Semicolon: links two related main clauses. I like tea; my brother prefers coffee.
• Colon: introduces a list or explanation.
• Dash: a dramatic pause. The door opened - and there stood the headteacher.

PERSUASIVE TECHNIQUES: AFOREST
Anecdote, Facts, Opinion, Rhetorical question, Emotive language, Statistics, Triples (rule of three)
Plus: direct address ("you"), imperatives ("Act now"), counter-argument then rebuttal.

STRONG OPENINGS
Start with a vivid scenario, a shocking fact or a question, not "I am going to talk about...".

SPELLINGS TO LEARN
accommodation, receive, believe, definitely, separate, embarrass, occurrence, rhythm

questions.question: Which is the strongest opening for a persuasive speech about school uniform?
options: I am going to talk about uniform.
Imagine walking into school and being judged for your clothes before you even speak.
questions.answer: Imagine walking into school and being judged for your clothes before you even speak.
questions.explanation: It hooks the audience with direct address and an emotional scenario.

questions.question: What is pathetic fallacy?
options: Weather or setting reflecting a character's mood
questions.answer: Weather or setting reflecting a character's mood
questions.explanation: e.g. rain and grey skies when a character is sad.

questions.question: Which is an oxymoron?
questions.explanation: An oxymoron puts opposite ideas together: deafening + silence.

questions.question: Which uses dashes correctly for a dramatic pause?
options: The door opened - and there stood the headteacher.
questions.answer: The door opened - and there stood the headteacher.
questions.explanation: A dash before the reveal creates suspense.

subject: Maths
title: Expanding, factorising and equations
body:
EXPANDING BRACKETS
Multiply everything inside by the term outside.
$5(x + 3) = 5x + 15$     $-2(x - 4) = -2x + 8$  (negative × negative = positive)

FACTORISING (the reverse)
Take out the highest common factor.
$12x + 18 = 6(2x + 3)$     $x^2 + 7x = x(x + 7)$

EQUATIONS WITH x ON BOTH SIDES
Get the x terms on one side first.
$7x - 4 = 3x + 20$
subtract $3x$: $4x - 4 = 20$
add 4: $4x = 24$
divide by 4: $x = 6$

EQUATIONS WITH BRACKETS
Expand first. $4(x - 2) = 2x + 6$ → $4x - 8 = 2x + 6$ → $2x = 14$ → $x = 7$

nth TERM
Difference first, then adjust. 11, 8, 5, 2: difference $-3$, so $14 - 3n$.
Check with $n = 1$: $14 - 3 = 11$ ✓

questions.question: Expand and simplify $5(x + 3) - 2(x - 4)$.
Work out $-6 \times 4 + 15$.
Factorise fully $12x + 18$.
questions.explanation: The highest common factor of 12 and 18 is 6: $6(2x + 3)$.

subject: Maths
title: Percentage change, angles and circles
body:
PERCENTAGE CHANGE
Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100
£40 → £46: change 6, $6 \div 40 \times 100 = 15\%$ increase

MULTIPLIERS
Increase by 12%: × 1.12.   Decrease by 20%: × 0.8
£250 increased by 12% = $250 \times 1.12 = $ £280

ANGLES IN PARALLEL LINES
• Alternate angles (Z shape) are equal
• Corresponding angles (F shape) are equal
• Co-interior angles (C shape) add up to 180°

POLYGONS
Exterior angles always add up to 360°.
Regular octagon: each exterior angle = $360 \div 8 = 45$°, so each interior angle = 135°.

CIRCLES
Circumference $= \pi d$ (or $2\pi r$)
Area $= \pi r^2$
Radius 5 cm: area $= 3.14 \times 25 = 78.5$ cm²

VOLUME OF A CUBOID
length × width × height, in cm³

questions.question: A price rises from £40 to £46. What is the percentage increase?
What is each exterior angle of a regular octagon?
questions.explanation: Exterior angles add to 360°: $360 \div 8 = 45$°.

questions.question: Two parallel lines are crossed by a straight line. One alternate angle is 65°. What is the other?
questions.explanation: Alternate angles (Z-angles) are equal.

questions.question: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are $x$ and 110°. Find $x$.
questions.explanation: Co-interior angles add to 180°: $180 - 110 = 70$°.

subject: Science
title: Digestion, respiration and electricity
body:
DIGESTION
mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine (nutrients absorbed) → large intestine (water absorbed)
Enzymes break big food molecules into small ones the body can absorb.

RESPIRATION (in every cell)
Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy)
Anaerobic (muscles, short of oxygen): glucose → lactic acid (+ less energy)

PHOTOSYNTHESIS (in plants)
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen  (needs light, happens in chloroplasts)

BREATHING
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli: oxygen into the blood, carbon dioxide out.

ELECTRICITY
Current (I) in amps, potential difference (V) in volts, resistance (R) in ohms.
$V = I \times R$, so $R = V \div I$.  6 V and 0.5 A → 12 Ω

MAGNETS
Like poles repel, opposite poles attract.

questions.question: Where is most water absorbed back into the body?
questions.explanation: The large intestine absorbs water from undigested food.

questions.question: What is produced by anaerobic respiration in human muscles?
questions.explanation: Without enough oxygen, muscles make lactic acid.

questions.question: What do enzymes do in digestion?
options: Break large molecules into small ones the body can absorb
questions.answer: Break large molecules into small ones the body can absorb
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts that break down large food molecules.

questions.question: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to release energy from glucose.

subject: Science
title: Atoms, elements, compounds and reactions
body:
ATOMS AND ELEMENTS
Everything is made of atoms. An element contains only one type of atom (iron, oxygen, carbon).
The periodic table lists all the elements. Metals: left and middle. Non-metals: right.
Elements in the same GROUP (column) react in similar ways.

COMPOUNDS
Two or more elements chemically joined. Water $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen.
Carbon dioxide $\text{CO}_2$: 1 carbon + 2 oxygen.

MIXTURE vs COMPOUND
Mixture: not joined, easy to separate (air, salt water).
Compound: chemically joined, new properties (water, salt).

CHEMICAL REACTIONS
reactants → products
magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide
Mass is conserved: atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed.

SIGNS OF A REACTION
gas given off, colour change, temperature change, new solid (precipitate) forms

questions.question: Elements in the same group of the periodic table ...
options: were discovered at the same time
questions.explanation: Elements in a group react in similar ways, e.g. the alkali metals.

questions.question: Where are the metals found on the periodic table?
options: On the left and in the middle
questions.answer: On the left and in the middle
questions.explanation: Metals are on the left and centre; non-metals are on the right.

questions.question: Magnesium burns in oxygen. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.

questions.question: What is an element?
options: A substance made of only one type of atom
questions.answer: A substance made of only one type of atom
questions.explanation: An element contains only one type of atom, e.g. oxygen or iron.

subject: English
title: Analysing texts like a GCSE student
body:
WHAT EXAMINERS WANT
Not just WHAT a technique is, but WHY the writer uses it and its EFFECT on the reader.

ADVANCED TERMS
• Juxtaposition: contrasting ideas side by side (four pages of jokes vs one line)
• Irony: the opposite of what's expected ("over by Christmas")
• Motif: a repeated image or idea
• Enjambment: a sentence running over a line break; Caesura: a pause mid-line

CONTEXT
When and why was it written? What did people believe then? Link it to the writer's message.

A STRONG PARAGRAPH (What, How, Why)
What: The writer shows the war slowly breaking the brother.
How: The contrast between "four pages of jokes" and a "single line" ...
Why: ... makes the reader feel the family's growing fear, which reflects how many families experienced the war.

EMBED SHORT QUOTES
Better: the "single line" letter suggests ...  Worse: copying a whole sentence.

questions.question: Why might knowing when a text was written help you understand it?
options: Attitudes and events of the time shape what the writer says
It gives you the word count
questions.answer: Attitudes and events of the time shape what the writer says
questions.explanation: Context explains the values and events behind a text.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the subjunctive mood?
options: If I was going, I'd tell you.
If I were you, I would apologise.
questions.answer: If I were you, I would apologise.
questions.explanation: 'If I were' is the subjunctive, used for hypothetical situations.

questions.question: What does "juxtaposition" mean?
options: Placing contrasting things side by side for effect
questions.answer: Placing contrasting things side by side for effect
questions.explanation: e.g. placing wealth next to poverty to highlight the difference.

questions.question: What is a motif?
options: The first line of a poem
A recurring image or idea in a text
questions.answer: A recurring image or idea in a text
questions.explanation: e.g. repeated images of light and dark.

subject: English
title: Writing with control and range
body:
SENTENCE VARIETY
• Start with a participle: Trembling, she reached for the handle.
• Short sentence for impact. Then a longer one that builds detail and rhythm.
• Relative clauses add detail: The book that I borrowed was brilliant.

PUNCTUATION RANGE
Semicolon; colon: dash - brackets ( ) - used deliberately, not just for decoration.

ARGUMENT WRITING
Introduction with a clear view → points with evidence → counter-argument and rebuttal → strong conclusion.
Use discourse markers: Furthermore, However, Consequently, Ultimately.

DESCRIPTIVE / NARRATIVE WRITING
Zoom in on small details. Use all five senses. Show feelings through actions, not labels.
Plan a structure: hook → build → turning point → resolution.

GRAMMAR FOR GCSE
If I were you (subjunctive for hypotheticals). Fewer (countable) vs less (uncountable).
Who (subject) vs whom (object).

questions.question: In an argument essay, what is a counter-argument?
options: An opposing view that you then respond to
questions.answer: An opposing view that you then respond to
questions.explanation: Acknowledging and rebutting the other side strengthens your argument.

questions.question: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation: A comma follows 'However' when it starts a sentence.

questions.question: Which sentence best shows a varied, ambitious opening?
options: Trembling, she reached for the handle.
questions.answer: Trembling, she reached for the handle.
questions.explanation: Starting with a verb ending -ing (a participle) is varied and vivid.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a relative clause?
options: The book that I borrowed was brilliant.
questions.answer: The book that I borrowed was brilliant.
questions.explanation: 'That I borrowed' adds information about the book.

subject: Maths
title: Indices, standard form and algebra
body:
INDEX LAWS
$x^a \times x^b = x^{a+b}$     $x^a \div x^b = x^{a-b}$     $(x^a)^b = x^{ab}$
$x^0 = 1$     $x^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{x}$

STANDARD FORM: $A \times 10^n$ with $1 \le A < 10$
46 000 000 = $4.6 \times 10^7$     0.00032 = $3.2 \times 10^{-4}$

DOUBLE BRACKETS (multiply every term by every term)
$(x + 3)(x + 5) = x^2 + 5x + 3x + 15 = x^2 + 8x + 15$

FACTORISING QUADRATICS
$x^2 + 7x + 12$: find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7 → 3 and 4
$= (x + 3)(x + 4)$

INEQUALITIES
Solve like equations: $3x - 4 < 11$ → $3x < 15$ → $x < 5$
(If you multiply or divide by a negative number, flip the sign.)

SIMULTANEOUS EQUATIONS
$x + y = 10$ and $x - y = 4$: add them → $2x = 14$ → $x = 7$, then $y = 3$

questions.question: Write 46 000 000 in standard form.
questions.explanation: The first number must be between 1 and 10: $4.6 \times 10^7$.

questions.question: Write $3.2 \times 10^{-4}$ as an ordinary number.
questions.explanation: Move the decimal point 4 places to the left: 0.00032.

questions.question: Solve $\dfrac{2x + 1}{3} = 5$.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 3: $2x + 1 = 15$, so $2x = 14$ and $x = 7$.

questions.question: Simplify $x^5 \times x^3$.
questions.explanation: Multiplying: add the powers, $5 + 3 = 8$.

subject: Maths
title: Graphs, Pythagoras and percentages
body:
STRAIGHT-LINE GRAPHS: $y = mx + c$
$m$ = gradient (steepness), $c$ = where it crosses the $y$-axis.
Gradient from two points = change in $y$ ÷ change in $x$
(1, 3) to (4, 12): $9 \div 3 = 3$

PYTHAGORAS (right-angled triangles only)
$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, where $c$ is the hypotenuse (longest side, opposite the right angle)
Finding $c$: square, ADD, square root.  6 and 8 → $\sqrt{100} = 10$
Finding a shorter side: square, SUBTRACT, square root.  13 and 12 → $\sqrt{25} = 5$

VOLUME OF A PRISM / CYLINDER
Volume = area of cross-section × length.  Cylinder: $\pi r^2 h$

REVERSE PERCENTAGES
After a 20% increase the price is £60. £60 = 120%, so 100% = $60 \div 1.2 = $ £50

COMPOUND INTEREST
original × (multiplier)$^{\text{years}}$:  $1000 \times 1.1^2 = 1210$

questions.question: What is the gradient of the line $y = 4x - 7$?
questions.explanation: In $y = mx + c$, the gradient is $m = 4$.

questions.question: A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, 12). What is its gradient?
questions.explanation: Gradient = change in $y$ ÷ change in $x$ = $9 \div 3 = 3$.

questions.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Use $\pi \approx 3.14$.
questions.explanation: $V = \pi r^2 h = 3.14 \times 9 \times 10 = 282.6$ cm³.

subject: Science
title: Genetics, energy and forces
body:
DNA AND GENES
DNA is in the chromosomes inside the nucleus. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a characteristic.
Body cells: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). Sex cells: 23.

VARIATION AND EVOLUTION
Inherited (eye colour) vs environmental (scars, language).
Natural selection: the best-adapted individuals survive, reproduce and pass on their genes.

ENERGY
Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (h)
Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in  (500 J in, 400 J useful → 80%)

ELECTRICITY
$P = I \times V$  (power = current × potential difference)

FORCES AND MOTION
$F = m \times a$  (force = mass × acceleration)
Density = mass ÷ volume

WAVES
Sound: longitudinal. Light and all EM waves: transverse.
EM spectrum: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma

questions.question: What is the power of a device with current 5 A and potential difference 230 V?
questions.explanation: $P = I \times V = 5 \times 230 = 1150$ W.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
questions.explanation: Body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); sex cells have 23.

questions.question: Which of these is caused only by genes (inherited)?
questions.explanation: Natural eye colour is inherited; the others depend on the environment.

questions.question: What does 'natural selection' mean?
options: Individuals best suited to their environment survive and pass on their genes
questions.answer: Individuals best suited to their environment survive and pass on their genes
questions.explanation: Better-adapted individuals are more likely to survive and reproduce.

subject: Science
title: Atomic structure and equations
body:
INSIDE THE ATOM
Nucleus: protons (+1) and neutrons (0). Shells: electrons (−1).
Atomic number = number of protons. Neutral atom: protons = electrons.

THE PERIODIC TABLE
Group 1 (alkali metals): very reactive, react with water to make hydrogen. More reactive going DOWN.
Group 7 (halogens): reactive non-metals. Less reactive going down.
Group 0 (noble gases): unreactive, full outer shells.

BALANCING EQUATIONS
Same number of each atom on both sides; change only the big numbers in front.
$2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$  (4 H and 2 O each side)

REACTIVITY SERIES (most → least)
potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold

THE ATMOSPHERE
78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, about 1% argon, about 0.04% carbon dioxide.
More $\text{CO}_2$ traps more heat → global warming.

questions.question: An atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does a neutral atom of it have?
questions.explanation: Neutral atoms have equal numbers of protons and electrons.

questions.question: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons; electrons orbit in shells.

questions.question: Group 1 metals (e.g. sodium) are stored in oil. Why?
options: They react quickly with air and water
questions.answer: They react quickly with air and water
questions.explanation: Alkali metals react vigorously with oxygen and water.

questions.question: What is the charge on an electron?
questions.explanation: Protons are +1, neutrons 0, electrons −1.
